# Models {#sec-models}

::: {.callout-note}
Drafted in part by LLM-based AI tools (Claude Code/Opus 5).
:::

To describe trajectories of word learning, we must estimate the number of words children understand, say or sign at different ages. Averages are insufficient: families and practitioners also want to know ranges -- the extents to which children tend to differ at each age. Our target is therefore the distributions of word counts at monthly age intervals, describing both typical counts and the spreads around them.

Previous research, personal experience and evident constraints can inform our expectations. When children are beginning to learn their first words, counts must sit close to zero, so the distribution starts narrow. Children then learn new words at different rates, so as the typical count rises with age, the differences between children compound and the distribution widens. Counts are also bounded -- a child cannot know fewer than zero words, and a checklist cannot record more words than it contains. Vocabulary grows gradually, word by word, so we can expect the distribution to shift and spread smoothly with age rather than to make large jumps over short periods. A statistical model lets us state these expectations precisely and combine them with our data to estimate the distributions we are seeking.

This section introduces our statistical approach -- what statistical models can and cannot claim, and how Bayesian inference expresses uncertainty, uses existing knowledge and supports prediction -- and then describes the models we fit and the assumptions underpinning them.

## Statistical modelling and Bayesian inference

Statistical modelling and inference offer methods for defining mathematical models and fitting them to data to estimate values of interest [@coxPrinciplesStatisticalInference2006; @gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020; @chanStatisticalModelingComputation2025]. They are central to evaluating scientific theories and interpreting data, and can express what a theory means more precisely than words alone [@farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018, chapter 1].

Statistical models do not by themselves explain how the world works, though they can evaluate the predictions of models that do. A regression model reveals statistical relationships between predictors and outcomes, but those relationships acquire their real-world relevance only within an empirical model -- an account of the real-world phenomenon that informs which statistical and process models can test it [@spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @vanoijenBayesianCompendium2024; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018].

The mapping between the two runs both ways: one empirical model admits many statistical models, and one statistical model is consistent with many empirical models. So even when a statistical model fits the observed data well, we cannot be certain its motivating explanation is 'the right one' — another, equally credible, explanation may fit just as well:

> "Many models correspond to the same hypothesis, and many hypotheses correspond to a single model. This makes strict falsification impossible." [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020, page 4]

Developing and evaluating models is therefore continual and iterative: a competing model may explain the data better, and new observations refine existing models, revise theories and motivate new ones [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

### Different approaches

There are different approaches to statistical inference, differing in their philosophical and mathematical foundations and in the conclusions they license [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

Bayesian methods remain uncommon in developmental Down syndrome research, but for the questions this study addresses they offer four notable advantages: (1) probability statements that mean what most people take them to mean; (2) uncertainty expressed as full distributions; (3) a principled way to bring existing knowledge to bear; and (4) direct predictions about individual children [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @bernardoBayesianStatistics2025; @wagenmakersBayesianInferencePsychology2018; @wagenmakersBayesianFrequentistInference2008].

#### Probability as uncertainty

Bayesian inference treats probability as a measure of uncertainty about unknown quantities -- "relative, in part to this ignorance, in part to our knowledge" [@laplaceEssaiPhilosophiqueProbabilites1814] -- so that a number near one marks an event we consider very likely and a number near zero an event we consider very unlikely [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. On a partly cloudy day, "a 50% chance of rain this afternoon" means that, given what we currently know, rain and no rain seem about equally plausible.

Frequentist uncertainty is instead grounded in how an estimation procedure behaves across repeated samples. A confidence interval is not a probability statement about where the true value lies and does not rank some values as more plausible than others [@moreyFallacyPlacingConfidence2016] -- a distinction that is, unfortunately, often misunderstood [@hoekstraRobustMisinterpretationConfidence2014].

#### Estimates as distributions

Bayesian inference begins with a prior distribution -- what we consider plausible before seeing the data. It then uses Bayes' theorem to update the prior distribution with the data to yield a posterior distribution [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. A Bayesian posterior distribution supports direct and intuitive statements such as: "given our model and the data, the typical 36-month-old child with Down syndrome learns about 5 new words per month, with an 89% probability that the median rate lies between 2 and 7."

#### Using existing knowledge

A prior encodes what is plausible about each parameter before the current data are analysed. Priors can draw on previous research and the experience of people with relevant expertise, where this is available. A well-grounded prior combined with the data yields estimates that are more stable, and often more precise, than the data alone. This can be especially valuable when datasets are small or noisy and a substantial evidence base already exists [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020].

The need to specify a prior is sometimes criticised as subjective. However, all statistical analyses rest on assumptions [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. Arguably, Bayesian priors are more explicit and open to scrutiny. A prior "should be chosen, evaluated, and revised just like all of the other components of the model", and we can test directly how sensitive our estimates are to it [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. For this study, priors let us bring existing knowledge of vocabulary development to bear and improve the accuracy of our estimates.

#### Predictions for individual children

From the posterior we can also predict unobserved outcomes. Drawing parameter values from the posterior and simulating a new observation for each draw yields a *posterior predictive distribution* that carries both the randomness in the data and our uncertainty about the parameters [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. This supports statements such as: "given our model and the data, there is an 89% probability that a 36-month-old child with Down syndrome understands between 0 and 142 words" -- a statement that is directly useful for setting expectations about individual children.

#### Computation

Bayesian inference is centuries old [@bayesLIIEssaySolving1763; @LaplaceMemoireProbabilite; @laplaceTheorieAnalytiqueProbabilites1820]. For a while, the calculations required were prohibitive for all but the simplest models. However, this is no longer the case:

> "...this was solved in 1990 through the introduction of Markov chain Monte Carlo to use computational power rather than brute analytical derivation. We now exist in an era where there are no intellectual or analytical impediments to specifying and estimating Bayesian models." [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]

Today, modern sampling algorithms [@metropolisEquationStateCalculations1953; @hastingsMonteCarloSampling1970; @hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014], are packaged in freely accessible open-source tools such as Stan and PyMC with interfaces to R and Python [@standevelopmentteamStanLanguageReference2026; @abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023]. Bayesian analysis is consequently now used across economics, political science, ecology, biology, neuroscience, medicine, psychology and education research [@gillBayesianModelingInference2020; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @bonBeingBayesian2020s2023; @pfadtMethodologicalMetamorphosisRapid2025].

## Outcomes {#sec-outcomes}

Vocabulary checklists record a subset of the words a child understands, speaks or signs (@sec-data) at a point in time. Each item is a true or false (checked or not checked) option. A child's score is a count of true responses out of $n$ checklist items. One completion of a checklist (an *administration*) yields up to one count per *outcome* (understood, spoken, signed) for a child of a given age. Each such count (one child, one age, one outcome) is an *observation*. We write $W$ for an observed count, subscripted by outcome where the distinction matters: $W_{\text{understood}}$, $W_{\text{spoken}}$ and $W_{\text{signed}}$. Our statistical models must consider how observations are distributed.

### A single reference inventory {#sec-reference-inventory}

Our pooled data include forms with varying numbers of lexical items[^lexical-items] (@sec-data). Checklists are designed to sample the words children learn earliest, and shorter forms are typically given to younger children. Therefore, for a child with an item count well below a form's maximum, the items a shorter form omits are mostly items that the child does not yet know. Given this, a count recorded on a shorter form will be close to the count a longer checklist would have recorded. We therefore score every count against a single reference inventory of $n = 810$ lexical items, whichever form recorded it, so that every estimate is on the same scale.

[^lexical-items]: Vocabulary checklists contain lexical items presented in a single citation form -- typically the singular form for nouns and the base form for verbs. They do not list all word forms and so cannot count, for example, understanding “pea” and “peas” as understanding two words. 

This approximation is less accurate for children near the maximum of a shorter form, who may know words their form does not ask about but that would have been identified on a longer form. To evaluate the assumption, we examine how often pooled counts approach their form's maximum, test whether raw counts or proportions of each form's maximum better align counts recorded on different checklists, and refit models using only the counts recorded natively on the 810-item checklists.

#### Counts near maxima

Counts near the maximum of a shorter form are uncommon among the data we have pooled for children with Down syndrome: 42 of 977 observations of words understood (4.3%, five of them at the maximum itself) and 18 of 1,428 observations of words spoken (1.3%) fall within 90% of a shorter form's maximum, and none of the 904 observations of words signed do.

The typically developing pool relies on the approximation more heavily. Here, every observation comes from a shorter form (@sec-data). Most sit well below their form's maximum, because the pool is restricted to ages 8 to 30 months and each form is designed for the ages at which it is given. The exception is spoken vocabulary towards the top of that window, where typically developing children can approach their form's ceiling: 4.0% of the pool's spoken observations fall within 90% of their form's maximum -- negligible below 22 months, 3.5% at 22 to 25 months, 7.7% at 26 to 27 months, and about one in five observations at 28 to 30 months. Words understood show the same pattern on a smaller scale: 3.8% overall, rising above 20% only at 23 to 25 months, the oldest ages of the longest-running comprehension form (the 418-item Oxford CDI). A count at a shorter form's ceiling is censored: the child is credited with every word the form asks about, and under the same easiest-first approximation would have been credited with at least as many — and plausibly more — items on the reference inventory. Because the model treats such counts as exact, estimated counts at the oldest typically developing ages are more likely to understate than overstate the count the reference inventory would have recorded. This is a statement about the reference-inventory count, not about spoken vocabulary at large; what checklist counts can and cannot say about vocabulary beyond the words checklists sample is discussed in @sec-data.

#### Forms align more closely on raw counts than on proportions

Two checks support scoring raw counts against the reference inventory rather than rescaling each count in proportion to its form's length. First, one study assessed 34 children on both the 810-item DSE checklists and the 416-item Oxford CDI (@sec-data). A measurement model fitted to these dual-form administrations estimates the ratio of the two forms' counts at matched age: for words understood it runs from about 0.9 at the youngest dual-form ages to 1.4 by 49 months -- close to the value of 1 that our common scoring assumes over the ages at which shorter forms are typically given -- and it everywhere excludes the 1.95 that rescaling in proportion to form length (810/416) would imply. The rise with age is the compression described above: as the shorter form runs out of items, it records progressively fewer of the words a longer checklist would have identified. Second, if shorter forms sampled words in proportion rather than easiest-first, counts recorded on shorter forms would sit systematically lower. They do not: across the typically developing pool, the median counts of words understood in different languages align more closely on raw counts than on proportions of each form's maximum at every age from 8 to 15 months, and the shortest form (309 items) does not record the lowest counts.

#### Sensitivity analysis

Finally, we conducted a sensitivity analysis where models were refitted using only the administrations recorded natively on the 810-item DSE checklists, so that no count is scored against a maximum its form did not use. This restriction keeps 278 of the 1,521 administrations in the Down syndrome pool (194 children from four sources, spanning 9 to 115 months), so the restricted fits inform the comparison only where their coverage overlaps the full pool's.

### A Beta-Binomial distribution {#sec-betabinomial}

The words on a checklist are fixed. Therefore, a count $W$ can take only integer values $0 \le W \le n$, and the corresponding proportion $p$ is bounded accordingly. Our outcome model should respect these constraints: counts are discrete, non-negative and bounded above. Since every count in our data is scored against the reference inventory (@sec-reference-inventory), we define $n = 810$.

A count of true responses out of $n$ items follows a Binomial distribution when two assumptions hold within an administration: that (a) given the probability of a true response $p$, the item responses (words checked) are independent; and that (b) every item carries that same probability. This gives a mean of $np$ and a variance (fixed by the mean) of $np(1-p)$ [@gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020, sec. 3.2]. We then assume the same distribution holds across administrations: that (c) the probability is the same for every observation of a given outcome at the same age.

Under the Binomial model, given our inventory of $n = 810$ words, and with $p = 0.3$, the expected count is $np = 243$ with a variance of $np(1-p) = 170.1$, a standard deviation of about 13 words. Vocabulary scores vary far more *between* children of the same age than this common probability will allow [@galeoteAcquisitionProductiveVocabulary2008; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023; @zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013]. A Beta-Binomial model relaxes assumption (c) by allowing the probability for each observation to vary: rather than one probability shared by all children of an age, each observation's probability is drawn from a Beta distribution [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013, sec. 17.2; @qiaoBetaBinomialModelCount2025].

A Beta-Binomial model also covers departures from assumption (a). Within an administration, responses are unlikely to be truly independent. If one parent completes the whole form, then anything that sways their judgement (for example, a generous or a cautious reading of what counts as "says") sways all the items together. The Beta-Binomial makes no distinction between the two failures: exactly the same distribution of counts arises whether each administration has its own probability or the items within an administration move together, so the two stories cannot be told apart from counts alone. Both are absorbed into the same fitted dispersion.

### The sufficiency of counts

For vocabulary checklists, assumption (b) is false: words differ in difficulty, and some are learned earlier than others. We rely on this ordering to justify our single reference inventory (@sec-reference-inventory), and a hypergeometric test against the three DSE checklists rejects equal item probabilities decisively (TODO: ref/appendix). Nonetheless, under an item-response model in which words differ in difficulty but separate children equally well, the total score carries all the information in the item responses about the child's underlying vocabulary ability. Two children with the same count are indistinguishable on ability, whichever words make it up, and on a given set of items a higher count always implies a higher estimate of ability. Modelling counts rather than individual words therefore discards nothing about the quantity we care about (for this study). Checklist items will not separate children exactly equally well, so this argument is an approximation; its cost cannot be measured from counts alone -- a count that carries all the information about ability carries none about the items.

Moreover, unequal item difficulty makes little difference to the distribution of the count. For a single observation -- one child's count on one occasion -- unequal difficulty lowers the variance rather than raising it. A child's count has the Binomial variance computed at their average item probability, minus $n$ times the variance of their item probabilities around that average. On its own scale this reduction is not small. It matters little, however, because the within-observation component is the minor share of the total variance: at every age, most of the variation in counts lies between children, so even a large error in the smaller component moves the total standard deviation by no more than a few per cent, largest at the youngest ages (TODO: pin the variance shares and worst case; appendix). In any case, the Beta-Binomial cannot express a variance below the Binomial's -- the Binomial is its floor -- so the reduction is absorbed into the fitted dispersion, one reason we later read dispersion as a property of the count distribution rather than a measurement of children (@sec-kappa).

### The limitations of counts

However, there are limits to what any count can tell us. A count is not an interval measure: equal differences in words do not reflect equal differences in underlying ability (a child's second hundred words may come more easily or less easily than the first). In addition, the scale is compressed near the floor and ceiling of the reference inventory, where large differences between children produce small differences in counts.

Change measured in raw words is therefore not comparable across ages or between children at different levels. Progress is better read as position relative to peers than as a number of words gained; centiles too are a ranking rather than a unit, locating a child within the distribution rather than measuring an amount of growth.

### The outcome model

For the reasons discussed in the preceding sections, we model each count as Beta-Binomial with mean proportion $p$ and concentration $\kappa$:

$$
W \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}(n,\,p,\,\kappa),
\qquad
\alpha = p\,\kappa,
\qquad
\beta = (1 - p)\,\kappa,
$$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the Beta distribution's conventional shape parameters, related to ours by $p = \alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$ and $\kappa = \alpha+\beta$.

Here $p$ is the expected proportion of the inventory checked, so the expected count is $\mathrm{E}[W] = np$. The concentration $\kappa$ controls the extra spread: as $\kappa$ grows large the Beta-Binomial approaches the Binomial; as it shrinks, counts spread more widely around the same mean $np$. This extra variation describes observations around a population trajectory. It should not be confused with uncertainty about the trajectory itself.

Where a model estimates several outcomes jointly (@sec-joint-outcomes), parameters carry the outcome's subscript: $p_{\text{understood}}$ is the expected proportion for the count $W_{\text{understood}}$, and likewise the concentration $\kappa_{\text{understood}}$.

### Age-varying dispersion {#sec-kappa}

For observation $i$ at age $x_i$ months we standardise age,

$$
z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{\sigma_x},
$$

so that a one-unit change in $z$ corresponds to $\sigma_x$ months. This scale differs by population and model (identical $z$-scale priors imply different smoothness assumptions in months for different models), and is primarily a computational convenience: the samplers and the Gaussian process approximation (@sec-hsgp) work with centred inputs of unit order.

Spoken vocabulary counts are more dispersed at older ages than at younger ones [@berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001; @galeoteDevelopmentVocabularySpanish2011; @marchmanMacArthurBatesCommunicativeDevelopment2023; @zampiniLexicalSyntacticDevelopment2011]. We therefore let the conditional dispersion vary smoothly with age:

$$
\kappa(z) = \kappa_{\min} + \exp\!\left(a_\kappa + b_\kappa z\right).
$$

The two terms do separate jobs. The exponential term rises or falls smoothly with age -- by a constant multiple for each $\sigma_x$ months, rather than a constant amount -- and can approach zero but never turn negative. The constant $\kappa_{\min}$ is therefore a floor: however extreme the age, the concentration never drops below it. Together they let the dispersion of counts grow with age and then level off, rather than growing without limit.

## Trends {#sec-trends}

The outcome models (@sec-outcomes) give each observation an expected proportion $p$. To investigate how that proportion changes with age, we model a central (mean) trajectory.

Proportions must lie between zero and one, and relating them to age with a straight line ($p = \beta_0 + \beta_1 z$, say) will eventually stray outside those bounds. We therefore build the trajectory on an unconstrained scale: a predictor $f(z)$ of standardised age (@sec-kappa), free to take any value, transformed by the logistic function,

$$
p(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f(z)\right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left(-f(z)\right)}.
$$

The logistic function returns a value between zero and one whatever the value of $f$. The inverse of this transformation is the *logit*, $\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\{p/(1-p)\}$.

Vocabulary development may not follow a straight line on the logit scale -- put another way, it is unlikely to perfectly match the S-shaped curve of the logistic function. We therefore give $f$ two parts -- a linear trend, which carries the overall rise with age, and a smooth departure $g$, which captures variations from that trend:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(z) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 z + g(z),\\
g(z) &= \eta\, g_{\mathrm{unit}}(z), \qquad
g_{\mathrm{unit}} \sim \mathcal{GP}\!\left(0,\, k(\cdot,\cdot)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

### Flexible variations from the central trajectory

The departure $g$ is a Gaussian process (GP): a probability distribution over smooth functions [@rasmussenGaussianProcessesMachine2008; @schulzTutorialGaussianProcess2018]. We give it a mean of zero because any non-zero mean would be indistinguishable from the linear trend itself. Positive $g(z)$ therefore means the population mean at that age sits above the line, and negative $g(z)$ that it sits below; where data are sparse, the posterior pulls $g$ back toward zero and the straight line does the work alone.

A GP is specified by its kernel $k(z, z')$, which sets how strongly the departure at one age resembles the departure at another: ages close together take similar values, ages far apart are nearly unrelated. We use the radial basis function (exponentiated-quadratic) kernel with its variance fixed at one,

$$
k(z,z') = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z-z')^2}{2\ell^2}\right),
\qquad k(z,z) = 1,
$$

and carry the size of the departures in a separate amplitude $\eta > 0$. The two parameters then have separate jobs: the length-scale $\ell$ governs how quickly the curve can bend with age (large $\ell$, long slow bends; small $\ell$, rapid wiggles), while $\eta$ governs how far it can sit from the line. The kernel treats all ages alike -- the curve is permitted the same local smoothness at 36 months as at 72 -- and is flexible enough to approximate any smooth trajectory given enough data, which suits developmental curves whose precise shape is not known in advance.

#### HSGP approximation {#sec-hsgp}

Exact GP inference requires an $O(n^3)$ Cholesky factorisation. With several hundred observations per model this is feasible but costly inside MCMC, so we use the **Hilbert-space GP (HSGP)** approximation [@solinHilbertSpaceMethods2020; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022], a finite basis-function representation that generates $g_{\mathrm{unit}}$ from a unit-variance kernel and then rescales by $\eta$. Approximation quality depends on the basis size $m$ (accuracy vs cost), the boundary factor $c$ (the approximation domain, $c$ times the half-range of the standardised evaluation grid about its midpoint, must cover every point the basis is evaluated at), and the length-scale $\ell$ (shorter scales need more basis functions). We select $m$ and $c$ following PyMC's `approx_hsgp_hyperparams` recommendations for the specified range of $\ell$ [@abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023; @riutort-mayolPracticalHilbertSpace2022].

### Slope anchors {#sec-anchors}

Rather than placing weakly interpretable priors directly on $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$, we parameterise the linear trend through the expected proportion of words at two reference ages $x_a < x_b$. With $z_a = (x_a - \bar{x})/\sigma_x$ and $z_b = (x_b - \bar{x})/\sigma_x$, and priors placed on $p_{x_a}$ and $p_{x_b}$,

$$
\beta_1 = \frac{\operatorname{logit}(p_{x_b}) - \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a})}{z_b - z_a},
\qquad
\beta_0 = \operatorname{logit}(p_{x_a}) - \beta_1 z_a .
$$

This gives an interpretable baseline on the logit scale while the GP captures smooth departures.

The reference ages and the priors on $p_{x_a}, p_{x_b}$ are model-specific (e.g. 24 and 84 months for the Down syndrome models; 12 and 26 months for the typically developing models) [**TODO**: cross-reference].

## Joint outcomes {#sec-joint-outcomes}

The core structure described in the preceding sections is our starting point, used unchanged by our base models with single outcomes: VG01 (words spoken) and VG02 (words understood) for Down syndrome, and VG03 (words spoken) and VG04 (words understood) for typically developing children. The remaining models estimate two or three outcomes jointly. 

### Production nested within understanding

The joint models use the fact that production is logically nested within understanding. They estimate the expected proportion of words understood, $p_{\text{understood}}(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f_{\text{understood}}(z)\right)$, together with the *production ratio* -- the expected fraction of understood words that are also spoken:

$$
q(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(h(z)\right),
\qquad
p_{\text{spoken}}(z) = p_{\text{understood}}(z)\,q(z),
$$

where $f_{\text{understood}}$ and $h$ are logit-scale age predictors, each built as in @sec-trends (a linear trend plus a smooth GP departure): $f_{\text{understood}}$ carries the age profile of the proportion understood, and $h$ that of the production ratio. Both factors lie between zero and one, so expected spoken vocabulary can never exceed expected understood vocabulary.

The nesting also holds count by count, not only in expectation. When an administration records both counts, we model the pair in two steps that mirror how the words relate. The first step models the understood count, out of the full inventory of $n$ items. The second models the spoken count out of the $W_{\text{understood}}$ words that child understands -- not out of $n$ -- with $q$ as the expected proportion of them spoken:

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{\text{understood}} &\sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(n,\, p_{\text{understood}},\, \kappa_{\text{understood}}\right),\\
W_{\text{spoken}} \mid W_{\text{understood}} &\sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(W_{\text{understood}},\, q,\, \kappa_{\text{spoken}}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the two steps gives a single, coherent probability for the observed pair, and the constraint $0 \le W_{\text{spoken}} \le W_{\text{understood}} \le n$ is respected automatically: the model cannot produce a spoken count exceeding the understood count, because the spoken words are drawn from the understood ones. (The rare recorded pairs that violate the constraint are handled separately, below.) $q$ is therefore a genuine conditional proportion for paired, nested counts, not a ratio imposed on marginal means, and each outcome keeps its own age-varying dispersion (@sec-kappa).

@fig-joint-generative shows this structure. Age shapes spoken vocabulary through two routes: by growing the understood vocabulary from which spoken words are drawn, and by changing the fraction of understood words that are spoken.

![The joint model's generative structure. A paired observation's age determines the expected proportion understood and the production ratio; the understood count is drawn from the full inventory, and the spoken count from the child's understood words. Boxes are observed quantities; rounded nodes are latent ones.](diagrams/fig-joint-generative){#fig-joint-generative width="85%"}

This is the model's data-generating graph, not a causal diagram of development. The direction of the factorisation follows the logical nesting of the outcomes -- a child's spoken words are a subset of the words they understand -- and whether comprehension causally enables production is a developmental question these cross-sectional models do not address.

Note also the arrow the diagram does not contain: $q$ varies with age but, given age, not with the size of the child's understood vocabulary -- the understood count affects the spoken count only as the pool of words the ratio applies to. Two same-age children who understand 100 and 400 words are given the same expected production ratio. Whether the ratio additionally depends on comprehension itself is a question we return to with the cross-lag model (VG16).

### What the production ratio is -- and is not

Two properties of $q$ belong here, at its definition, rather than in a later caveat, because both bear on every comparison the report makes with it.

**$q$ is a composition-weighted average, not an item-level probability.** Its definition -- the fraction of understood words that are also spoken -- invites reading $q$ as the probability that a given word is spoken once understood. It is not that. Words differ markedly in difficulty (@sec-betabinomial), and children at a given age understand different numbers of words and different *sets* of words, so $q$ averages the per-word production probability over whatever vocabulary each contributing child happens to have. Two populations can differ in $q$ purely because their understood vocabularies are composed differently, with no difference in how readily any particular word is produced. The sufficiency argument in @sec-betabinomial is also the proof that this cannot be repaired within a sum-score model: a statistic sufficient for ability carries no information about item composition.

**A contrast at matched comprehension is not a contrast at matched age.** Where the report compares Down syndrome and typically-developing children at the same level of comprehension, the two groups are **8–13 months apart in age** at that matched level. A difference in $q$ read off such a comparison is therefore a difference between groups that are simultaneously unlike in age and in vocabulary composition, and neither can be held fixed while varying the other. Both qualifications apply wherever $q$ is reported.

### Signed words

The signing models add an analogous *sign ratio*:

$$
r(z) = \operatorname{logistic}\!\left(f_{\text{signed}}(z)\right),
\qquad
p_{\text{signed}}(z) = p_{\text{understood}}(z)\,r(z),
$$

with the parallel conditional likelihood $W_{\text{signed}} \mid W_{\text{understood}} \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(W_{\text{understood}},\, r,\, \kappa_{\text{signed}}\right)$. Unlike the other predictors, $f_{\text{signed}}$ replaces the single linear trend with a three-anchor, piecewise logit-linear *tent* -- young, peak and older reference levels -- plus the usual GP for smooth departures. This allows signing to rise and then decline without making the GP alone carry the entire shape.

VG14 treats speaking and signing as conditionally independent given understanding. VG15 instead estimates their association, from the four pooled sources that record production word by word in both modalities rather than as marginal totals: uk_02, uk_07 and es_01 give, for each understood word, whether the child signs it, says it, does both or neither -- directly in the first two, and by subtraction from recorded totals in es_01 -- while nz_01 gives, within produced words, whether each is spoken, signed or both. These compositions are scored with a Dirichlet-Multinomial term in place of separate spoken and signed likelihood contributions, while the understood likelihood remains, because each composition is conditional on its observed total. The association carries a study-level random term: the informing sources disagree by more than sampling error, and with only four of them the between-study spread is itself weakly identified, so the per-study values rather than the pooled centre are the primary read wherever the association is reported. Which sources' signing fields measure total signed vocabulary -- and which are masked, or reintroduced only as sensitivity analyses -- is a data question, addressed in @sec-data.

### When only one count of a pair is recorded

When the understood count is unavailable, the spoken or signed count remains usable through a marginal fallback,

$$
W_{\text{spoken}} \sim \mathrm{BetaBinomial}\!\left(n,\, p_{\text{understood}}\,q,\, \kappa_{\text{spoken}}\right),
$$

and analogously for signing. A recorded spoken or signed count greater than its understood count is retained through the same fallback and counted as a source-data violation in the fit log rather than silently discarded.

The fallback reuses the conditional branch's dispersion $\kappa_{\text{spoken}}$, and that is an approximation: on conditional rows the dispersion is variation in $q$ alone, whereas fallback rows also absorb unobserved variation in $p_{\text{understood}}$. The size of the approximation is bounded exactly: the true marginal of a fallback row is more dispersed than the fallback's Beta-Binomial precisely when $q\,\kappa_{\text{spoken}} > \kappa_{\text{understood}}$ -- the level $p_{\text{understood}}$ drops out entirely -- and the two variances are equal on the boundary.[^fallback-moments] The fallback is therefore neither conservative nor anti-conservative as a structural matter: which way a given model errs is a question about its fitted concentrations. Three registered sensitivity analyses bound it in practice -- dropping the fallback rows altogether, giving the fallback branch its own dispersion through a single signed scalar that nests the default at zero, and replacing the fallback's dispersion with the one matching the true marginal's first two moments -- and posterior-predictive calibration is reported separately for the conditional and fallback rows, which differ systematically in age and study composition.

[^fallback-moments]: Binomial thinning collapses the paired factorisation to $W_{\text{spoken}} \mid \theta_{\text{understood}}, \theta_{\text{spoken}} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(n,\, \theta_{\text{understood}}\theta_{\text{spoken}}\right)$, so the true marginal of a fallback row is a Binomial mixed over the *product* of two independent Beta variates. That product is not itself Beta, but both its moments are elementary, and comparing them with the fallback's reduces to the single condition given here.

## Multilevel models

To separate the population age curves from differences in study composition and from repeated measurements on the same child, we add random intercepts on the logit-scale predictors at the observation level. For a predictor $f_\bullet \in \{f_{\text{understood}}, h, f_{\text{signed}}\}$,

$$
f_\bullet(z_i) \;\to\; f_\bullet(z_i) + \delta^{\text{study}}_{\bullet,\,s(i)} + \delta^{\text{subj}}_{\bullet,\,j(i)},
\qquad
\delta_\bullet \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \tau_\bullet),\ \ \tau^{\text{study}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(0.5),\ \ \tau^{\text{subj}}_\bullet \sim \mathrm{HalfNormal}(1.5),
$$

implemented non-centred, where $s(i)$ and $j(i)$ index the study and subject of observation $i$. The two levels take different scales because they are on different scales in the data: fitting the same grouping structure outside the models puts the between-child standard deviation at 0.74–1.15 on the logit scale across the family, where between-study differences are around a third of that. Study intercepts absorb between-lab/between-study level differences; subject intercepts stop within-child repeated measurements being treated as independent. **The reported population curves set every random effect to zero**, so their interpretation is unchanged. Tiny studies can be trimmed before fitting (`min_study_observations`) to avoid near-unidentified intercepts.

The TD hierarchical models apply the same repeated-measures rule. VG11 and VG12 include a child intercept on their single outcome, and VG13 includes child intercepts on both $p_{\text{understood}}$ and $q$. A fixed-seed sensitivity retains one randomly selected administration per study-specific child and disables the child effects, providing a cheaper check that conclusions do not depend on treating repeat administrations as additional independent children.

#### Levelling the trend above the high anchor {#sec-clamp}

The Down syndrome joint models evaluate the trajectory over 8–115 months while their anchors sit at 24 and 84, so about a quarter of the domain lies above the high anchor, where no prior constrains the trend. On the logit scale a line steep enough to climb between the anchors saturates over that distance. Extrapolated to 115 months, VG10's production-ratio mean alone reaches 0.993 — $P(\text{mean} > 0.99) = 0.90$ across the posterior — against a realised 0.842. The GP is then spent hauling the mean back, $-3.3$ logits at the top of the range, while sitting idle ($+0.08$) at 48 months where the data are.

We therefore level the trend off above the high anchor, replacing $z$ in the linear term with

$$
z_{\text{eff}} = z_b - \frac{1}{s}\operatorname{softplus}\!\big(s\,(z_b - z)\big),
\qquad s = \frac{50}{z_b - z_a},
$$

so the mean rises linearly below $z_b$ and flattens above it, leaving the GP free to carry departures rather than correct an asymptote. The same coordinate is used for the projection basis in @sec-gpanchor, so the two constraints stay consistent.

Three properties are deliberate. **The clamp is one-sided:** below the low anchor the line extrapolates accurately — VG10's production ratio at 12 months is 0.019 by extrapolation against 0.022 fitted — and clamping there would instead pin young-age values at the 24-month level, which is much worse. **The transition is smooth rather than a hard minimum:** $\min(z, z_b)$ is continuous but its derivative jumps at the anchor and the fitted curve inherits a visible elbow, which in the first VG10 refit made the spoken trajectory briefly non-monotone, falling from 428.6 words at 84.3 months to 426.6 at 85.6. **The softness is scale-free:** setting $\beta$ from the anchor span makes the largest departure from the hard-clamped form $\beta_1 \log 2 / \beta$, or 1.4% of the anchor span — about 0.8 months of age for the Down syndrome models — whatever the age standardisation.

The cost is that $p_{x_b}$ is no longer exactly the mean at the high anchor age, falling short by that same amount. Between the anchors the mean is untouched, so both anchor priors carry over unchanged.

This applies to the Down syndrome joint and signing models (VG05, VG07–VG10, VG14–VG16 and VG20, which inherits VG10's setting), set by `clamp_mean_above_hi_anchor` in each model definition. The typically developing models do not use it: their evaluation domains extend barely beyond their high anchors. The univariate Down syndrome baselines, VG01 and VG02, extrapolate the line across the full domain.
